Diagnostic: plot the per-parameter error vs CRB std. A k1/k4 error much greater than 2% while k2/k3 are near 0.5% would indicate approximation-limited rather than noise-limited behaviour.
data.if_fails: Shows that the learned map is sample-limited. One could then generate additional simulated training data via context.forward in a custom_solver, which is allowed since only simulated data is used, or rely on hybrid refinement. It quantifies how much of the gap to the CRB is approximation error.

author: researcher-ml
title: Amortised learned init + short posterior-mean LM refinement reaches near-CRB accuracy (hybrid)
text: A torch_mlp trained on log-features with log-targets and noise augmentation, used as initializer for <=15 bounded LM iterations in log-space with a posterior_mean (importance-sampled MMSE) readout, achieves val rel_l2 <= 0.03, i.e. within ~1.6x of the CRB floor (0.0185), and strictly below the pure amortised MLP. Harness diagnostics give a CRB rel_l2 floor of ~0.0185 with Fisher condition ~62, so the problem is locally well-posed and noise-limited at sigma=0.001. Amortised regressors pay an approximation error from finite data (3000 samples) on top of the noise error; a few Gauss-Newton steps through the exact forward model can remove that approximation error locally, provided the init lands in the basin. Rel_l2 is a squared-error metric, so an MMSE readout should beat the mode where the posterior is truncated by the box (k1,k4 least determined, near bounds). The learned init falls inside the local convergence basin of LM (local Lipschitz stability holds near the truth). The posterior is close to Gaussian in log-k away from the box edges so the Laplace-based importance sampler is effective. Forward-model budget allows ~15 iterations on 750 val samples within 120 s across workers.

assumptions: The learned init falls inside the local convergence basin of LM (local Lipschitz stability holds near the truth).
The posterior is close to Gaussian in log-k away from the box edges so the Laplace-based importance sampler is effective.
Forward-model budget allows ~15 iterations on 750 val samples within 120 s across workers.
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid vs the same torch_mlp init alone. Hypothesis is falsified if hybrid val rel_l2 > 0.03 or if it is not at least 20% better than the init alone.
data.if_fails: If hybrid ~= init alone, the MLP already sits near the noise floor (approximation error is not the bottleneck). If hybrid is much worse than the CRB but better than init, LM is stalling at box bounds for k1/k4 or the init falls outside the basin, motivating more extra_starts or a mode readout comparison.

author: researcher-ml
title: Pure amortised MMSE: noise-augmented MLP on log-features reaches target without forward-model refinement
text: A squared-loss torch_mlp with log-target and heavy noise augmentation (noise_aug=4) approximates the posterior mean E[k|y] well enough to achieve val rel_l2 <= 0.05 using only simulated training data, but stays >= 1.3x above the best hybrid (i.e. above ~0.024). A squared-loss regressor trained on (theta, F(theta)+noise) pairs drawn from the prior converges to the Bayes posterior mean; noise augmentation multiplies the effective sample count of the noise distribution, reducing variance in the learned map. The inverse map here is smooth (4 parameters, moderate conditioning), so a 3000-sample MLP should at least clear the 0.05 target. This tests how much the forward-model refinement is actually buying, and gives a cheap amortised estimator. The inverse map theta(y) is smooth enough on the prior box that 3000 (x5 augmented) samples suffice for an MLP. Harness noise augmentation uses sigma matching the stated 0.001 measurement noise (noise_scale=1.0). Log-target compresses the dynamic range of k in [0.5,2] and equalises relative error across segments.

assumptions: The inverse map theta(y) is smooth enough on the prior box that 3000 (x5 augmented) samples suffice for an MLP.
Harness noise augmentation uses sigma matching the stated 0.001 measurement noise (noise_scale=1.0).
Log-target compresses the dynamic range of k in [0.5,2] and equalises relative error across segments.
data.falsifiable_test: Falsified if val rel_l2 > 0.05 (amortised MMSE insufficient for target) or if val rel_l2 is within 1.1x of the best hybrid (refinement is unnecessary).
data.if_fails: If > 0.05, approximation error from limited training data dominates; next steps are hybrid refinement or generating extra simulated training data via a custom_solver using context.forward. If it matches the hybrid, the problem is noise-limited at the amortised level and the cheap estimator should be preferred.

author: researcher-experimental
title: MMSE readout beats the MLE mode at the box edges: learned init + LM refinement with posterior-mean estimator
text: A hybrid estimator will reach val rel_l2 below the 0.0193 achieved by bounded log-space MLE in a prior run. It uses an extra-trees initializer, followed by log-space LM refinement through the forward model, and reads out the posterior mean (importance sampling on the Laplace approximation under the uniform box prior) instead of the mode. The gain should come mostly from k1 and k4. Those are the least-determined parameters (CRB rel std about 0.02). Near the box bounds, the mode is pinned or truncated, while the box-truncated posterior mean shrinks error under squared loss. The metric is a squared-error-type loss (rel_l2), so the Bayes-optimal point estimate is the posterior mean, not the mode. The noise is small (sigma=0.001) and the Fisher condition number is moderate (about 62), so the posterior is close to Gaussian in the interior. In that region, mode and mean should agree and both sit near the CRB floor of about 0.0185. The prior is uniform on [0.5, 2], so a non-trivial fraction of draws have k1 or k4 within a few posterior standard deviations of a bound. There the Gaussian posterior is truncated, and the MMSE estimate can beat the MLE because it is biased toward the interior. This is a measurement-limited regime where the estimator choice, not the model class, should be the remaining lever. The learned init exists to cut LM iterations so the run fits the 400 worker-second budget, and to avoid any spurious local minima. The harness forward model is the same explicit FD simulator (40 points, 200 steps) that generated the data, so there is no model-form error. The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=0.001, so the Gauss-Newton Laplace approximation is a reasonable importance-sampling proposal. The val split draws k from the stated i.i.d. uniform prior, so the box-truncation effect is present at the expected frequency. The extra-trees initializer lands within the LM basin of attraction, with initializer error well below 0.1 rel_l2. The posterior is unimodal at this noise level. If it is not, Laplace-based importance sampling underestimates the MMSE benefit.

assumptions: The harness forward model is the same explicit FD simulator (40 points, 200 steps) that generated the data, so there is no model-form error.
The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=0.001, so the Gauss-Newton Laplace approximation is a reasonable importance-sampling proposal.
The val split draws k from the stated i.i.d. uniform prior, so the box-truncation effect is present at the expected frequency.
The extra-trees initializer lands within the LM basin of attraction, with initializer error well below 0.1 rel_l2.
The posterior is unimodal at this noise level. If it is not, Laplace-based importance sampling underestimates the MMSE benefit.
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of this hybrid (posterior_mean) against the prior-run MLE value of 0.0193. If budget allows, also compare against the same hybrid with estimator=mode. Additionally, stratify per-parameter error by whether the true k1 or k4 lies within 0.1 of a bound. The hypothesis is falsified if overall val rel_l2 is at least 0.0193, or if the mean-versus-mode improvement is not concentrated in the near-boundary stratum for k1 and k4.
data.if_fails: If mean and mode tie, the box-truncation effect is negligible at sigma=0.001, and about 0.019 is the practical floor for this sensor layout. Further gains would then require better measurement design (more sensors nearer the ends, or a longer time window), not a better estimator. If the result is worse than the MLE, the Laplace importance-sampling proposal is miscalibrated near the bounds.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Amortised MMSE without the forward model at inference: a noise-augmented MLP on raw sensor traces reaches the 0.05 target
text: A torch MLP trained on the 3000 simulated training pairs, with squared loss on log-k and noise augmentation matched to sigma, will reach val rel_l2 at or below 0.05. It needs no per-sample forward solves at prediction time. Because the noise is small relative to the signal, the remaining error should be dominated by function-approximation error from the finite training set, not by the noise. This predicts a large gap above the 0.019 physics floor while still beating the 0.05 target. This is the data-driven control arm that the physics result needs. A squared-loss regressor trained on samples from the prior and noise model approximates the posterior mean directly. If it reaches 0.05 or lower, the amortised route is viable and much cheaper per sample. If it fails, the inverse map is too nonlinear or ill-conditioned for 3000 samples, and that tells us how much of the physics method's advantage comes from using the forward model. Noise augmentation (fresh noise draws at the same sigma) tests a specific data-distribution claim. With only 3000 trajectories, one noise realisation per sample lets the network overfit to particular noise patterns, whereas resampling noise enforces the correct likelihood. Raw features with standard scaling are appropriate because sensor amplitudes decay smoothly. Log targets match the positivity constraint and the multiplicative scale of k. noise_aug with noise_scale=1.0 adds fresh Gaussian noise at the stated sigma=0.001 on the raw features, before scaling. 3000 prior draws cover a 4-D parameter box densely enough for a smooth MLP interpolant. That is roughly 7 points per axis on a full grid, and probably sufficient given how smooth the forward map is. Train and val come from the same prior and simulator, so there is no distribution shift. The k-to-observation map is smooth (the FD solution is analytic in k on the box), so the inverse is smooth wherever the Fisher information is well conditioned.

Train and val come from the same prior and simulator, so there is no distribution shift.
The k-to-observation map is smooth (the FD solution is analytic in k on the box), so the inverse is smooth wherever the Fisher information is well conditioned.
data.falsifiable_test: Train on the train split only and evaluate val rel_l2. The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 is above 0.05. Secondary check: report per-parameter relative error. The prediction is that the k1 and k4 errors are each at least twice the k2 and k3 errors, mirroring the CRB ordering. If instead the errors are uniform across segments, approximation error rather than information content dominates.
data.if_fails: If val rel_l2 is above 0.05, the amortised map is sample-limited for the weakly informed edge segments. Physics or hybrid refinement through the forward model is then necessary, not optional. The next step would be to generate more simulated training data via context.forward (allowed, since it is simulation only) or to use the MLP only as an initializer. If the MLP succeeds but the k1/k4 error ratio is uniform, the network is underfitting k2 and k3, and capacity or epochs, not information, is the bottleneck.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Amortised init + forward-model MMSE refinement: closing the gap from the MLP (≈0.025) to the CRB floor (≈0.0185)
text: The best amortised network (torch_mlp raw+pca48+logy, val rel_l2≈0.0247) is limited by approximation error, not by noise. A few bounded LM steps through the exact forward model, started from that network, followed by an importance-sampled posterior mean, will remove most of the approximation error. This should bring val rel_l2 to ≤0.022, i.e. within ~20% of the CRB floor of 0.0185. Two research traditions disagree on framing. The ML view says the squared-loss network already is the MMSE estimator. The inverse-problems view says the network is only an approximate MMSE, and with σ=0.001 the likelihood is sharp enough that per-sample local refinement dominates. The CRB floor (0.0185) sits below the observed MLP error (0.0247), so roughly 25% headroom remains, and it can only be harvested by using the forward model. Using posterior_mean rather than mode matters because the metric is squared-error-like. Near the box edges (k1 and k4 are least determined) the MLE is pushed against the bounds, and the box-truncated posterior mean shrinks correctly. The MLP initialiser lands inside the LM basin of attraction for nearly all samples. The Gauss-Newton/Laplace approximation is adequate for importance sampling at σ=0.001, given Fisher condition number ~62. The forward-model call budget covers 750 val samples × ~15 iterations × Jacobian evaluations within 120 s on 6 workers (explicit FD, 40×200 grid, is cheap).

assumptions: The MLP initialiser lands inside the LM basin of attraction for nearly all samples.
The Gauss-Newton/Laplace approximation is adequate for importance sampling at σ=0.001, given Fisher condition number ~62.
The forward-model call budget covers 750 val samples × ~15 iterations × Jacobian evaluations within 120 s on 6 workers (explicit FD, 40×200 grid, is cheap).
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid against its own initialiser in the same run. The hypothesis is refuted if the hybrid is not at least 10% better than the init, or if val rel_l2 > 0.022.
data.if_fails: If refinement gives no gain, the MLP is already near the Bayes risk and the CRB-based floor is misleading (Laplace/CRB overstates what is achievable, or the residual error is noise-limited). If refinement makes things worse, the landscape has spurious minima near the init, or the IS posterior mean is miscalibrated.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: No learning at all: per-sample box-constrained posterior mean through the forward model already beats the amortised network
text: Training on 3000 simulations is unnecessary because the forward model is available, cheap and well-conditioned. Per-sample bounded LM in log-k space with a few multistarts, followed by the importance-sampled posterior mean, should reach val rel_l2 < 0.024, at or below the best data-driven model, with zero training data. If multistart from the prior centre fails on a non-negligible fraction of samples, that falsifies the claim that the misfit is effectively unimodal on [0.5,2]^4. This challenges the 'supervised regression' framing of the task. For a 4-parameter problem with an exact simulator, the natural estimator is Bayesian inversion per sample, and the 3000-sample training set is a distraction. It also tests the unresolved hypothesis m-261109-54edbdef, which was critiqued (m-261109-c68594a4) but never executed. It isolates how much of proposal 1's gain comes from the forward model versus the initialiser. The least-squares misfit in log-k is unimodal, or 3 starts suffice, on the prior box. Diffusion smoothing does not create flat valleys along k1/k4 that trap LM before 25 iterations. The compute budget covers 750 × 3 starts × 25 iterations.

assumptions: The least-squares misfit in log-k is unimodal, or 3 starts suffice, on the prior box.
Diffusion smoothing does not create flat valleys along k1/k4 that trap LM before 25 iterations.
The compute budget covers 750 × 3 starts × 25 iterations.
data.falsifiable_test: Run on val and report the fraction of samples whose best-start residual exceeds noise level (normalised χ² > 1.5), together with the val rel_l2. The hypothesis is refuted if rel_l2 ≥ 0.0247 (the best MLP) or if more than 2% of samples show non-converged or high-χ² fits.
data.if_fails: If it fails through local minima or slow valleys, the learned initialiser is essential and proposal 1's framing is right. If it converges but rel_l2 is still above the MLP, the Laplace-IS posterior mean is miscalibrated relative to an amortised MMSE, which argues for trusting the network's implicit prior averaging.

text: convergence of Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with bounds The gradient of f is Lipschitz continuous with constant L. The Hessian approximations are bounded above and below by positive constants. The sequence of parameters produced by the algorithm is bounded. The estimator converges almost surely to the true parameter as the sample size increases. This holds under specific conditions on the parameter bounds and the assumptions of a referenced theorem. The parameter values are constrained within a defined interval. The result applies to a particular estimator defined in a prior equation. The function L is bounded above and below by expressions involving the Frobenius norm of the estimated parameter matrix. The upper bound is a linear function of the squared norm plus a constant. The lower bound is the squared norm itself. The function L is bounded in probability if and only if the parameter estimate is bounded in probability. An estimable parameter is bounded.

text: Levenberg-Marquardt convergence piecewise constant conductivity parabolic inverse problem For a specific domain and background conductivity, a certain regularization functional is defined. The theorem establishes the existence of constants that satisfy a variational source condition. The convergence rate is given by a logarithmic function involving several parameters. The result applies under certain smoothness assumptions on the true conductivity. Under certain conditions, the Levenberg-Marquardt method converges to a solution. The operator derivative is uniformly bounded, and a tangential cone condition holds. If the initial guess is sufficiently close to the solution, the method converges. The discrepancy principle is used to select the regularization parameters. The Levenberg-Marquardt iterates converge to a solution of the problem under the given assumptions and exact data. The true conductivity lies in a specific set. The derivative of a matrix function is continuously differentiable and satisfies a bounded divergence condition. Under two possible boundary conditions for the conductivity, the error in the L2 norm between successive iterates and the true conductivity decreases linearly. This linear convergence holds for appropriate choices of constants.

text: MLP init (log-target, noise-augmented), followed by 12 bounded log-space LM iterations with a Laplace-IS posterior-mean readout, reaches val rel_l2 < 0.021. The per-parameter RMS relative errors are within 1.3x the CRB rel std (k1 2.15%, k2 0.58%, k3 0.52%, k4 1.74%), and chi2/dof is in [0.85, 1.15]. These conditions show the arm is noise-limited, not convergence-limited. Pilot: 0.0184 on 60 val, chi2/dof 0.94, z_rms 1.00, and a forward model consistent with the data (residual std 0.00099). At sigma=0.001 the problem is locally well-conditioned (Fisher condition ~62). An estimator reaching the noise floor should therefore show chi2/dof ~1 and error/CRB ratios ~1. The posterior mean under the uniform box prior is the Bayes estimator for squared error. Near the edges it can beat the CRB through bias, which matters for k1/k4. context.forward equals the data simulator (confirmed by the pilot: residual std 0.00099 vs 0.001). The likelihood is locally unimodal around the learned init (pilot chi2/dof 0.94 is consistent with this, but it is not proven globally). The Laplace proposal is adequate for IS (pilot ESS 58/128 at the last sample; per-sample distribution unknown). The per-sample posterior rel std (~1-2%) makes the E[k|y] vs rel_l2-Bayes-rule difference negligible.

It also cuts the excess over the P-001 hybrid by at least 40% relative to the n=3000 MLP control (P-006). Squared-loss regression on prior-predictive pairs targets E[k|y]. Its excess risk over the Bayes risk decays with n. A 2-point learning curve (P-006 at n=3000, this arm at n=9000) tells approximation-limited behaviour, where error decreases, apart from noise-limited or capacity-limited behaviour, where it stays flat. author: researcher-experimental
title: Paired readout control: same learned init + LM, estimator=mode, against the merged posterior-mean hybrid; the gain must sit in the boundary stratum
text: Hold the init and LM fixed and change only the readout from mode to posterior mean. The mean should then lower squared error only for val samples whose true k1 or k4 lies within 0.1 of a bound (about 25% of samples under the uniform prior). In that boundary stratum, the per-sample MSE reduction should be at least 10%. In the interior stratum, the change should be within ±2%. The aggregate rel_l2 gain should be 0.5-3%. This mode arm should itself land at val rel_l2 between 0.0185 and 0.0205, which replicates the remembered 0.0193 MLE anchor on the same split. The metric is squared-error-like, so the posterior mean is Bayes-optimal. In the interior, the near-Gaussian posterior makes mode and mean coincide. At the support boundary, the mode gets pinned while the truncated-posterior mean is pulled inward, and the CRB, which bounds only unbiased estimators, no longer constrains it. With a shared init and identical samples, this is the cleanest falsifiable test of 'estimator choice is the remaining lever'. It also replaces an unverified cross-run anchor with a same-split measurement. The harness forward model is the data-generating explicit FD simulator, so there is no model-form error. The explicit scheme is stable up to k=2. If it were not, the data would show it too. Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=0.001. Val k values are i.i.d. uniform on [0.5, 2]^4. The posterior-mean readout uses self-normalised importance sampling with zero prior weight outside the box, not clipping. The merged posterior-mean hybrid (P-001/P-003/P-007) is run with the identical init spec, transform, iterations and tikhonov=0, so the contrast isolates the readout. LM from the MLP init converges to the same mode in both arms, because the init error of about 0.025 is well inside the basin.

text: A torch MLP trained on the 3000 training pairs with log targets and noise augmentation at sigma will reach val rel_l2 in [0.022, 0.030]. Its excess over the CRB floor of 0.0185 comes from function-approximation error at n=3000, not from noise. This shows up as error/CRB ratios that are largest for k2 and k3 (2 or more) and smallest for k1 and k4 (about 1.2-1.6), with every ratio above 1.2 in the interior stratum. This is the data-driven control the physics and hybrid claims need, and it is also the init-only error of the shared hybrid init. A parameter-uniform approximation floor added in quadrature to parameter-specific noise floors predicts inverted ratio ordering. Pure noise-limitation predicts flat ratios of about 1. The two explanations make opposite, testable predictions. noise_aug=2 with noise_scale=1.0 adds fresh N(0, 0.001^2) noise to the raw features before scaling. Train and val share the prior and the simulator, so there is no shift. The forward map is smooth (analytic in k on the box under a stable explicit scheme), so its inverse is smooth where the Fisher matrix is well conditioned (median condition number 62). Approximation error is roughly uniform in relative terms across segments, because the network has no segment-specific inductive bias.

title: No learning at all: per-sample box-constrained posterior mean through the forward model (full-val confirmation of pilot 0.0184)
text: Training data are unnecessary for accuracy. Per-sample bounded LM in log-k with 3 starts and 25 iterations, followed by a box-truncated Laplace-IS posterior mean, reaches val rel_l2 < 0.0225 on the full 750-sample val set. This is at least 9% better than the 0.0247 MLP anchor. The log-k misfit is effectively unimodal on [0.5,2]^4: at most 2% of samples have chi2/dof (N-4) > 1.5, or have a best start different from the first start. The pilot on 60 val samples gave 0.0184, calibrated uncertainties (z_rms 1.00, 2-sigma coverage 0.96) and chi2/dof 0.94, and took 3.6 s. A full-val run costs about 45 s and turns a suggestive pilot into a decision. If confirmed, the 'supervised regression' framing is not needed for accuracy: the amortised networks only buy inference speed. The final model should then be the physics estimator, or a hybrid chosen only for speed. The log-k misfit is unimodal on the box, or 3 harness-chosen starts suffice. The Laplace approximation is adequate for IS at sigma=0.001. The pilot ESS was 58/128, which supports this. The forward-model budget covers 750 x 3 x 25 evaluations, about 270k forward-equivalent calls, extrapolating from 21.5k calls for 60 samples.

data.if_fails: If rel_l2 is >= 0.0225 but chi2 is fine, the 60-sample pilot was optimistic, and the gap to the MLP is within noise. In that case, choose between the physics estimator and a hybrid by cost. If the chi2 or start-dependence criterion fails, there are local minima or flat valleys in k1/k4, and the learned init (P-001) is essential for robustness.

text: convergence of Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with bounds The gradient of f is Lipschitz continuous with constant L. The Hessian approximations are bounded above and below by positive constants. The sequence of parameters produced by the algorithm is bounded. The estimator converges almost surely to the true parameter as the sample size increases. This holds under specific conditions on the parameter bounds and the assumptions of a referenced theorem. The parameter values are constrained within a defined interval. The result applies to a particular estimator defined in a prior equation. The function L is bounded above and below by expressions involving the Frobenius norm of the estimated parameter matrix. The upper bound is a linear function of the squared norm plus a constant. The lower bound is the squared norm itself. The function L is bounded in probability if and only if the parameter estimate is bounded in probability. An estimable parameter is bounded.

This uniqueness holds modulo phase rotations. The condition on mu is sharp. The loss function has no misleading local minima when the number of measurements is sufficiently large relative to the signal dimension. The global minima correspond exactly to the true signal and its negative. Every other critical point is a strict saddle. This holds with high probability under Gaussian measurements. Under certain assumptions and conditions, a global minimizer is the unique solution to the minimization problem. There exists a positive constant and a radius such that the function value exceeds the minimum by at least a quadratic bound. This holds for all points within the specified distance from the minimizer. The result ensures local strong convexity around the unique minimizer. If certain conditions from a previous theorem hold and a specific quadratic form is positive for all directions, then a given point is the unique global solution to a trust region problem.

title: TheoremSearch: self-normalized importance sampling truncated Gaussian posterior mean bias near support boundary
text: self-normalized importance sampling truncated Gaussian posterior mean bias near support boundary The bias of a truncated normal random variable is bounded by an expression involving the mean and variance. The bound depends on the truncation threshold and the distance between the mean and the threshold. Specifically, the absolute bias is at most four times the absolute mean multiplied by an exponential decay term. The decay term involves the squared difference between the truncation threshold and the absolute mean, scaled by twice the variance. Under certain assumptions, the integral over the complement of a ball around the maximum likelihood estimator decays as order n to the power of negative p plus epsilon with high probability. The ratio of this integral to the full normalizing constant is of order n to the power of negative p over two. These results hold when using a specific truncation parameter defined by the logarithm of n. The bounds demonstrate the concentration of the posterior distribution. The truncated posterior distribution is defined on a measurable set. If the true parameter is not in the set and the set is bounded, the posterior converges to a uniform measure over that set as the sample size grows. If the set is unbounded, the posterior converges to the zero measure. These results hold under specific assumptions. The theorem establishes bounds on the normalized bias of an estimator over a class of data generating processes. The processes satisfy boundedness and smoothness conditions on the covariate density and conditional mean functions, along with a boundary condition on the kernel. As the sample size grows and the bandwidth shrinks, the supremum of the normalized bias over the boundary region converges to a constant of order one. The lower and upper limits of this normalized bias are bounded above and below by constants proportional to one.

title: Theorem 2 (Approximation Bias: Uniform Guarantee) — Estimation and Inference in Boundary Discontinuity Designs: Distance-Based Methods
text:
The theorem establishes bounds on the normalized bias of an estimator over a class of data generating processes. The processes satisfy boundedness and smoothness conditions on the covariate density and conditional mean functions, along with a boundary condition on the kernel. As the sample size grows and the bandwidth shrinks, the supremum of the normalized bias over the boundary region converges to a constant of order one. The lower and upper limits of this normalized bias are bounded above and below by constants proportional to one. For some $L > 0$, let $\mathcal{P}$ be the class of data generating processes satisfying Assumptions \ref{assump: DGP}(i)-(iii) with $\mathcal{X}\subseteq [-L,L]^2$, Assumption \ref{assump: Kernel, Distance, and Boundary}, and the following three additional conditions:\begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont (),noitemsep,leftmargin=*]\item $L^{-1} \leq \inf _{\mathbf{x}\in \mathcal{X}} f_X(\mathbf{x}) \leq \sup _{\mathbf{x}\in \mathcal{X}} f_X(\mathbf{x}) \leq L$, 

\item $\max _{0 \leq |\boldsymbol {\nu }| \leq p} \sup _{\mathbf{x}\in \mathcal{X}} |\partial ^{\boldsymbol {\nu }} \mu _t(\mathbf{x})| + \max _{0 \leq |\boldsymbol {\nu }| \leq p} \sup _{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in \mathcal{X}} \frac{|\partial ^{\boldsymbol {\nu }} \mu _t(\mathbf{x}) - \partial ^{\boldsymbol {\nu }}\mu _t(\mathbf{y})|}{\| \mathbf{x}- \mathbf{y}\| } \leq L$, and 

\item $\liminf _{h\downarrow 0}\inf _{\mathbf{x}\in \mathcal{B}} \int _{\mathcal{A}_t} k_h(\d(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{x})) d \mathbf{u}\geq L^{-1}$. 

\end{enumerate}For any $p\geq 1$, if $nh^2\to \infty $ and $h\to 0$, then\begin{align*}  1 \lesssim \liminf _{n\to \infty } \sup _{\P \in \mathcal{P}} \sup _{\mathbf{x}\in \mathcal{B}}\frac{\mathfrak {B}(\mathbf{x})}{h} \leq \limsup _{n\to \infty } \sup _{\P \in \mathcal{P}} \sup _{\mathbf{x}\in \mathcal{B}}\frac{\mathfrak {B}(\mathbf{x})}{h} \lesssim 1. \end{align*}

text: Per-sample |k_hat_hybrid - k_hat_physics| on the 60 pilot samples For a fixed k and policy π, with probability at least 1 minus δ prime, the difference between Φ_k and its estimate is bounded by a constant times A H squared D over η, multiplied by the square root of log 2 over δ prime divided by N. The constant C is a universal numerical value. The quantities Φ_k and its estimate are defined in earlier equations. The hat value for the square symbol is approximately one minus four over two to the k, with an error term of order k over four to the k. The hat value for f is nearly the same as for the square symbol, differing by order k over four to the k. The hat value for b sub one is close to one with error order k over two to the k, while for r sub one it is two over two to the k times one plus order k over two to the k. The sum of differences for f and r is bounded by order k over two to the k times the difference in dot p for f, and the L1 norm of the difference in hat p is bounded by order k squared over two to the k times the L1 norm of the difference in dot p. The difference between f_k and its average is bounded by a term involving the sample size and constants. The two-norm difference between g_k and its average is bounded by a similar expression. The two-norm difference between H_k and its average is also bounded by a comparable term. Each bound depends on the proportion of data not used in the respective subsample. The absolute difference between H_k and Z^* is bounded by the supremum of the absolute difference between the sample average of h and Z over x. The expected squared difference between H_k and its mean is at most the variance of H_k. This variance is bounded by the expected squared difference between H_k and Z^*. That expected squared difference is at most the expected squared supremum of the absolute deviation between the sample average of h and Z.

Assuming $\dot{q} _1,\dot{q} _2\in \bm{\Gamma} $, \begin{equation} \label {e:BP_hatvalue} \begin {array}{rl} \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} _i( up{ tt{$\square$}} ) \hspace {-6pt}&= 1 -4/2^k + O(k/4^k),\\ \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} _i( up{ tt{f}} ) \hspace {-6pt}&= \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} _i( up{ tt{$\square$}} ) + O(k/4^k),\\ \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} _i( up{ tt{b}} _ up{ tt{1}} ) \hspace {-6pt}&= 1 + O(k/2^k),\\ \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} _i( up{ tt{r}} _ up{ tt{1}} ) \hspace {-6pt}&= (2/2^k)[1 + O(k/2^k)]. \end {array} \end{equation} Further, writing $\Delta \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} (\cdot ) \equiv \hm ^\lambda (\cdot )|\hat{p} _1 (\cdot ) - \hat{p} _2 (\cdot )|$, \begin{equation} \label {e:BP_hatdif} \begin {array}{rl} \Delta \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} ( up{ tt{f}} ) + \Delta \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} ( up{ tt{r}} ) \hspace {-6pt}&= O(k/2^k)\Delta \dot{p} ( up{ tt{f}} ),\\ \|\Delta \hm ^\lambda \hat{p}  \|_1 \hspace {-6pt}&= O(k^2/2^k) \|\Delta \dot{p}  \|_1.\end {array} \end{equation} (Recall that $\hat{p} (\hat{\sigma} \oplus  up{ tt{1}} )=\hat{p} (\hat{\sigma} )$ and $\hm (\hat{\sigma} \oplus  up{ tt{1}} )=1-\hm (\hat{\sigma} )$, so $(1-\hm )^\lambda \hat{p} (\hat{\sigma} ) = \hm ^\lambda \hat{p} (\hat{\sigma} \oplus  up{ tt{1}} )$. text: The absolute difference between H_k and Z^* is bounded by the supremum of the absolute difference between the sample average of h and Z over x. title: TheoremSearch: Wall-clock time for 12000 vectorised context.forward calls
text: Wall-clock time for 12000 vectorised context.forward calls The algorithm outputs vectors with bounded expected operator norm, controlled by a term involving logarithms and dimension ratios. With high probability, the operator norm is also bounded by a similar logarithmic expression. The time required scales linearly with the product of dimensions and time steps. The gradient of the loss function with respect to the vectorized matrix variable can be computed efficiently. The computation time is bounded by the sum of two matrix multiplication complexities. These complexities depend on the dimensions n and d. The result holds under the given definitions of the input matrices and variables. For constant cost vectors, the problem can be solved with depth logarithmic in both dimension and time. The required work scales with dimension and a polynomial in time. The exponent in the time complexity depends on the matrix multiplication constant. An outer product update for vectors with non-negative entries is processed in time linear in the batch size plus the time to sort the vector dimension.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Learning-curve point n≈9000 with P-013's recipe: is the amortised-network gap to the CRB floor sample-limited?
text: With P-013's architecture and loss held fixed, adding 6000 fresh prior-predictive simulations (with per-epoch resampled sigma=0.001 noise) reduces val rel_l2 to < 0.0225. The excess MSE over the physics floor (P-014) shrinks by at least 30% relative to P-013 (n=3000). The pilots show the physics estimator sits at the CRB floor, about 0.0184. Any amortised-network gap is therefore approximation or estimation error of the map y -> E[k|y]. For a fixed function class, estimation error decays with n (roughly n^-1 for a parametric-rate excess risk). A capacity or optimisation floor would instead be flat in n. A 9k point between P-013 (3k) and P-011 (15k, same code) gives a 3-point curve and separates these two cases. The cost is low because forwards are cheap and inference needs no forward calls. This matters practically: if the gap closes, an amortised estimator can replace per-sample LM at test time. context.forward(theta) returns noise-free observations in the same flattened layout as the training features. The code checks the shapes and falls back to the given data only if they differ. The forward budget allows 6000 extra evaluations (the pilot used about 14k in seconds). P-013's torch_mlp internals (LayerNorm+GELU, AdamW, cosine) are reproduced closely enough. Remaining implementation differences, such as early-stopping details, are second-order compared with a 3x change in n. The harness rel_l2 is a vector-norm relative error. Excess is therefore measured in MSE on the metric's own scale, not against per-parameter CRB values.

data.falsifiable_test: Full val (n=750), paired against P-013 (same recipe, n=3000) and P-014 (physics floor) on identical samples. The hypothesis is falsified if either holds. (a) rel_l2 >= 0.0225. (b) Excess MSE (this minus P-014) is not at least 30% below P-013's excess, with the 95% paired-bootstrap CI of the reduction excluding 30%, or the reduction is smaller than 2x P-013's seed SD if that is reported. With P-011 at 15k on the same code, fit log(excess MSE) = a - alpha*log(n). alpha >= 0.5 supports the estimation-limited explanation. alpha < 0.2 indicates a capacity or optimisation floor. Diagnostics: excess stratified by distance to the box edges (k1/k4 boundary stratum vs interior), and per-sample error normalised by per-sample CRB at each val truth with the metric's vector-norm normaliser.
data.if_fails: If (a) and (b) both fail with alpha near 0, the amortised network is capacity- or optimisation-limited at this recipe. More simulated data is then wasted, and per-sample LM through the forward model (P-014) is the only route to the CRB floor. If (b) passes but (a) fails, the gap is estimation-limited but closes slowly; the fitted alpha gives the n needed for 0.0185 and lets us judge whether amortisation is worth it. If the excess concentrates in the boundary stratum, the limit is the network's representation of the truncated posterior mean near the edges, not sample size.
data.response_to_critic: All points accepted, with the following changes. (1) Architecture confound: I replaced the sklearn MLPRegressor with a torch network that reproduces P-013's recipe. That is 512-256-128, LayerNorm+GELU, AdamW lr 1e-3 / wd 1e-4, a cosine schedule, batch 128, standardised raw features, log-k targets standardised, and best-epoch selection on an internal simulated holdout. This also removes the counterexample of an sklearn optimisation plateau. One difference from P-013 remains and I state it openly. The 6000 simulated rows get fresh N(0, sigma^2) noise resampled every epoch, from stored noise-free forwards. The 3000 given rows keep their single realisation. This is the correct data law, but it is a stronger augmentation than noise_aug=2, so P-013 vs this arm varies n plus the augmentation scheme. I recommend P-011 run this exact code with n_extra=12000 so that the 9k and 15k points share the recipe exactly; the slope between them is then confound-free. (2) Merge with P-011: endorsed in that form, as one recipe and one shared val set. I fit log(excess MSE) against log(n) with P-014's MSE as the floor. (3) Seed variance: a single seed is a genuine limitation. I lowered the claimed resolv

author: researcher-ml
title: Learning-curve endpoint (n=15k): P-013-matched MLP trained on 3000 given + 12000 forward-simulated prior draws with per-epoch fresh noise
text: The gap between the amortised MLP and the CRB (P-013 vs the ~0.0185 floor) is mainly finite-sample approximation error. Under that explanation, the same architecture, loss and target transform trained on 5x more prior draws (fresh noise each epoch) reduces val rel_l2 by at least 15% relative to P-013, to below 0.025, with no forward calls at inference. The competing explanation is an optimisation/capacity floor at fixed width. It predicts a gain under 5% across n=3k (P-013), 9k (P-010) and 15k (this arm). Noise augmentation only resamples noise around the same 3000 thetas, so it cannot fill the 4-D parameter space more densely. Explicit FD on 40 nodes x 200 steps is cheap to batch-simulate, so more prior draws are an inexpensive way to approach the Bayes estimator amortisedly. Physics pilots already sit at the floor (0.0184). The remaining question is why amortised networks fall short, and this arm answers whether the cause is data or capacity. A 3-point learning curve with P-010 and P-013 separates the two explanations by the slope. context.forward(theta) returns noise-free observations in the same flattened layout as the raw features. This is verified on 64 train rows: the residual std must be < 5*sigma, else no simulated data is used and the arm reduces to a P-013 replicate. The residual is stored as model.resid. The forward budget allows 12000 extra simulations, issued in 6 batches of 2000. Simulated prior draws count as 'simulated data'. Val and test are never touched in fit; early stopping uses a 10% hold-out of the given train rows. The [256,256] LayerNorm-GELU net matches P-013. If capacity binds, the gain will be small, and that outcome is exactly the falsifier.

The [256,256] LayerNorm-GELU net matches P-013. If capacity binds, the gain will be small, and that outcome is exactly the falsifier.
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 against P-013 (same architecture, loss and target transform, n=3k, mean over 2 seeds) and against P-010 (n=9k) on the same val split. The data-limit hypothesis is falsified if the improvement over P-013 is < 15% or if val rel_l2 >= 0.025. The capacity/optimisation floor is supported if the three points differ by < 5%, i.e. within seed variance. Secondary test: report per-parameter error_j / CRB_j at each val truth for n=3k and n=15k. Under the data-limit explanation, all ratios should fall toward 1. If k2/k3 ratios fall while k1/k4 ratios do not, the weakly identified parameters are limited by something other than data. The arm is invalid if the logged resid >= 5*sigma (n_sim=0).
data.if_fails: A gain under 15% means the MLP-to-CRB gap is not a data limit. It is then an optimisation/capacity floor at this width, the Jensen explanation having been ruled out as negligible. Only forward-model refinement (P-009 hybrid, or P-014 physics) closes the gap, so amortised inference should be used only as an initializer. A residual >> sigma means the simulator and data mismatch, which would also invalidate the physics arms' noise model.
data.response_to_critic: (1) Jensen bias: accepted. With a posterior relative std of about 0.5-2%, the bias is about sigma^2/2, roughly 2e-4 or less. That is negligible against a 0.02 error, so it is removed as a competing explanation. The real alternative is now stated as an optimisation/capacity floor: at fixed architecture, the error would stay flat as n grows. (2) Runtime: accepted. The pilot must measure the time. I cut cost by matching P-013's smaller [256,256] network. Fallbacks are n_extra=6000 or epochs=40. The harness gives no timing module, so I cannot add a wall-clock guard inside the code. (3) Comparator: accepted, it is now P-013. The net mirrors the torch_mlp spec exactly: Linear-LayerNorm-GELU [256,256], AdamW lr 1e-3, wd 1e-4, cosine LR, log-target, standardised raw features. One difference remains. P-013 uses aug2 noise copies of the 3000 rows. Here the 3000 given rows are used as observed, and only the simulated rows get fresh noise. Adding noise to already-noisy rows would double their variance. The pilot should also run P-013 with 2 seeds, as the critic's missing control asks. (4) Forward-consistency residual: accepted. It is stored as model.resid and must be logged; the arm is invalid

author: researcher-experimental
title: Single data-driven control: noise-augmented MLP is approximation-limited, with per-sample error/CRB ratios inverting the CRB ordering
text: A torch MLP trained on 3000 training pairs, with log targets and noise augmentation at sigma, reaches val rel_l2 in [0.022, 0.030]. In the interior stratum (every edge parameter more than 2 posterior std from a bound), the per-sample RMS ratio r_j = err_j/CRB_j(k_i) satisfies r_k2, r_k3 ≥ 2 and r_k1, r_k4 in [1.0, 1.7]. The ordering inverts the CRB ordering, as predicted by a roughly segment-uniform approximation floor of about 0.008-0.012 relative error added in quadrature to parameter-specific noise floors. This is the data-driven control for the physics and hybrid arms, and the init-only error for P-009. The two candidate explanations make opposite predictions. Pure noise-limitation gives flat ratios of about 1. A uniform approximation floor gives ratios that are largest where the CRB is smallest (k2, k3). The learning-curve arms (P-010/P-011) then test whether that floor shrinks with n. noise_aug=2, noise_scale=1.0 adds fresh N(0, 0.001²) noise to the raw features before scaling. Train and val share the prior and the simulator, so there is no distribution shift. Under the i.i.d. uniform prior, the four log k_j targets have identical marginal variance, so target scale cannot cause differential underfitting. In the interior stratum the posterior is near-Gaussian, so the CRB is a valid first-order reference for an MMSE approximator. Near the bounds it is not, so the analysis there is excluded. Per-sample CRB_j(k_i) is taken from the Gauss-Newton std reported by the physics arm (P-015) on the same val samples. The forward map is smooth on the box, and the Fisher matrix is well conditioned (median condition number 62), so the inverse is learnable.

data.falsifiable_test: Train on train and evaluate on val. Report rel_l2, per-parameter relative RMSE, and the per-sample CRB ratios r_j for all samples and for the 2·sd interior stratum. The hypothesis is falsified if any of these holds: rel_l2 is outside [0.022, 0.030]; in the interior stratum, min(r_k2, r_k3) < 2 or max(r_k1, r_k4) > 1.7; or all four interior ratios lie within [0.9, 1.3], which would mean the network is noise-limited. If a second seed runs, the seed SE must be below 0.0015 for the band test to be decisive.
data.if_fails: If rel_l2 is above 0.030 or the edge ratios exceed 1.7, the network is sample-limited on the weakly informed edges, and the forward-model refinement or more simulated pairs (P-010/P-011) are required. If the ratios are flat at about 1 and rel_l2 is below 0.022, the network is already near-efficient, and the amortised-vs-physics gap is a noise or readout effect, not approximation. If the ordering is not inverted but all ratios exceed 1.2, the floor is not segment-uniform, for example because sensor layout gives the edges weaker features.

I also report the vector-norm rel_l2 separately, so the two are never conflated. I request that the harness confirm crb_rel was computed as a median over draws of sqrt(CRB_jj)/k_j. (2) Accepted. The interior 'ratio > 1.2' test compares an MMSE approximator with an unbiased-estimator bound. That is valid only to first order where the posterior is near-Gaussian, and it is now listed as an explicit assumption. The criterion is restricted to the 2·sd interior stratum, where the critic's point (4) on P-012 shows boundary bias is absent. (3) Cost: I cut epochs to 150. author: researcher-exploratory
title: Canonical physics arm: per-sample bounded log-LM + box-truncated Laplace-IS posterior mean on full val (merged P-008/P-014)
text: Without any training data, per-sample bounded LM in log-k (3 starts, 25 iterations) with a box-truncated Laplace-IS posterior mean reaches val rel_l2 < 0.0225 on all 750 val samples (refutation threshold), and in fact < 0.020 (near-floor diagnostic). The log-k misfit is effectively unimodal on [0.5,2]^4. At most 2% of samples have chi2/dof (dof = N-4) > 1.5. At most 2% have a later start that reaches a distinct estimate (max|delta log k| > 1e-3) with a chi2 at least 1 unit lower than start 1. The pilot (n=60) sits at the CRB-scale floor with calibrated uncertainty. A full-val run decides whether the supervised-regression framing is needed for accuracy at all. If it is not, amortised networks only buy inference speed, which changes what the final model should be. The misfit is unimodal on the box, or 3 starts suffice. The Laplace approximation is an adequate IS proposal at sigma = 0.001 (pilot ESS 58/128). The forward-call budget covers roughly 270k forward-equivalents.

assumptions: The misfit is unimodal on the box, or 3 starts suffice.
The Laplace approximation is an adequate IS proposal at sigma = 0.001 (pilot ESS 58/128).
The forward-call budget covers roughly 270k forward-equivalents.
data.falsifiable_test:
Run on all 750 val samples and report the following:
- rel_l2, with a bootstrap 95% CI.
- The per-sample chi2/dof distribution.
- The count of samples where a later start reaches a distinct estimate (max|delta log k| > 1e-3) with a chi2 at least 1 unit lower than start 1.
- Median and 5th-percentile ESS.
- Per-parameter error divided by the per-sample CRB std.
- Error stratified by distance to the lower and upper bounds.
The hypothesis is refuted if rel_l2 >= 0.0225, if more than 2% of samples have chi2/dof > 1.5, or if more than 2% have a distinct, better later start. A rel_l2 below 0.020 counts as near-floor.
data.if_fails: If rel_l2 >= 0.0225 but chi2 is fine, the pilot was optimistic, and the choice between physics and hybrid comes down to cost. If the chi2 or start criterion fails, there are local minima or flat valleys in k1/k4, and the learned initialiser (P-009) has genuine value.
data.response_to_critic:
(1) Duplicate of P-008: P-008 is withdrawn, and P-014 is now the single canonical physics arm. Per-sample estimates, chi2, ESS and start outcomes are logged so P-015 and P-016 can be paired with it.
(2) Ill-posed start criterion: I adopt the critic's definition. A start counts as 'different' only if its final estimate differs from start 1 by max|delta log k| > 1e-3 AND achieves a chi2 at least 1 unit lower.
(3) Loose threshold: a tighter diagnostic is added. rel_l2 < 0.020 means near-floor; 0.020-0.0225 means good but not at the floor. The refutation threshold stays at 0.0225.
(4) ESS question: I will report the median and 5th-percentile ESS over all 750 samples. A 5th percentile below 20 flags readout Monte Carlo error, which is tested directly in the new P-016.
(5) k1/k4 bounds: bounded LM plus box-truncated IS exploits the bounds. I also stratify error by distance to the bounds, separately for the lower and upper edges.
(6) CRB normalisation (portfolio missing control): the 0.0185 floor is a vector-norm rel_l2 aggregate, while the per-parameter values are relative stds. Error/CRB ratios will use per-sample CRB at each val truth, computed from the Jacobian at the truth, not the m

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Paired readout contrast: MLE (mode) vs box-truncated posterior mean, identical LM, stratified by lower/upper edge
text: With the LM configuration identical to P-014, the mode readout has an aggregate val rel_l2 0.5-2% higher than the posterior mean. The gain is significant in the edge strata (any k_j within 2 per-sample CRB-std of 0.5 or 2.0, mostly k1/k4), and larger at the upper edge, where posteriors are wider in absolute terms. In the interior stratum the paired 95% bootstrap CI of the squared-error difference contains 0. This is the only clean readout contrast once P-012 is withdrawn. It resolves the P-012/P-015 disagreement on gain size, and it replicates the remembered no-learning MLE anchor (about 0.0193) on this split. Both arms are evaluated on identical val samples, so the comparison is paired. Any MMSE benefit comes from posterior mass truncated at the box.

assumptions: Both arms are evaluated on identical val samples, so the comparison is paired.
Any MMSE benefit comes from posterior mass truncated at the box.
data.falsifiable_test:
Compute the paired per-sample difference in squared relative error (mode minus P-014), with a 2000-resample bootstrap, overall and per stratum: lower edge, upper edge and interior. Also report the fraction of modes exactly at a bound. The hypothesis is refuted under any of these conditions:
- The edge-stratum CI excludes a positive gain.
- The interior CI excludes 0.
- The aggregate gap lies outside [0, 3%].
data.if_fails: If the edge gain is null, the Laplace-IS readout adds nothing beyond clamping, and the cheaper MLE should be the final estimator. If the interior difference is significant, the IS readout is shifting interior estimates, which points to Monte Carlo error or miscalibration (see P-016).
data.response_to_critic:
(1) Gap too large: I accept the critic's back-of-envelope estimate. Bounded LM already clamps the mode at the box, which captures part of the truncation benefit. The prediction is revised to an aggregate gap of 0.5-2%.
(2) Noise-driven falsification: the test is now a paired bootstrap per stratum, not a raw 'mode not higher' comparison. Two significance criteria are now required: the boundary stratum must show a significant gain, and the interior CI must contain 0.
(3) P-012's analysis plan is adopted. Edge strata are split per parameter into lower and upper edges, because the absolute posterior width differs by about 4x. I also report the fraction of modes exactly at a bound.
(4) posterior_samples in mode: it is ignored for the point estimate. It is kept at the minimum of 32 so the spec stays valid and the uncertainty report remains comparable.
(5) k1/k4 bounds: the mode exploits the bounds only through clamping. That contrast with the truncated mean is exactly what this arm measures.
(6) LM literature: no new applicable theorem was retrieved. This arm uses the identical LM configuration, so the convergence behaviour cancels in the paired contrast.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: IS readout accuracy control: same LM, posterior_samples 512 vs 128, paired with P-014
text: At 128 importance samples, the posterior-mean readout's Monte Carlo error is negligible relative to the posterior width. Re-running P-014 with 512 samples changes aggregate val rel_l2 by less than 1% relative, the paired interior CI contains 0, and the per-sample estimate shift stays below 0.1 posterior std for 95% of samples. If instead the low-ESS tail (5th-percentile ESS < 20 at 128 samples) shows larger shifts, concentrated in edge samples, then the 128-sample readout is noisy exactly where the MMSE gain is supposed to live. The critic lists an IS readout accuracy check as a missing control. Without it, P-015's edge-stratum contrast cannot separate a real truncation benefit from Monte Carlo noise in the readout. The pilot reported the ESS of only one sample. This control also checks whether the near-floor 0.0184 depends on a lucky Monte Carlo draw. The LM stage is deterministic given the configuration, so only the readout differs from P-014. Quadrupling the IS samples cuts the Monte Carlo std of the mean by about 2x, enough to expose readout noise if it is material.

assumptions: The LM stage is deterministic given the configuration, so only the readout differs from P-014.
Quadrupling the IS samples cuts the Monte Carlo std of the mean by about 2x, enough to expose readout noise if it is material.
data.falsifiable_test:
Compare per sample against P-014 and report the following:
- The paired bootstrap CI of the squared-error difference, overall and in the lower-edge, upper-edge and interior strata.
- Per-sample |shift| divided by the Gauss-Newton posterior std.
- ESS quantiles at 512 samples.
The hypothesis is refuted if the aggregate rel_l2 changes by more than 1% relative, if the interior CI excludes 0, or if more than 5% of samples shift by more than 0.1 posterior std.
data.if_fails: If the shifts are material, the 128-sample readout is Monte Carlo-limited. P-015's edge contrast must then be read against the 512-sample arm, and the final estimator should use more samples or deterministic quadrature on the truncated Laplace Gaussian.

author: literature
title: Theorem 3.2 — A fresh look at nonsmooth Levenberg--Marquardt methods with applications to bilevel optimization
text:
A solution to a root problem lies within a set where a function is Newton-differentiable. Under uniform boundedness and full rank conditions on the Newton derivative near the solution, a local Levenberg-Marquardt method converges superlinearly from nearby starting points. With a null sequence of parameters, the algorithm either stops in finitely many steps or generates a superlinearly convergent sequence. If the function is Newton-differentiable of order one and the parameters are chosen appropriately, the convergence becomes quadratic. Let $M\subset \mathbb{R} ^p$ be a set such that a solution $ ar z\in \mathbb{R} ^p$ of \eqref {eq:root_problem} satisfies $ ar z\in M$. Assume that $\mathcal F $ is Newton-differentiable on $M$ with Newton-derivative $D_N\mathcal F \colon \mathbb{R} ^p	o \mathbb{R} ^{q	imes p}$. We assume that there are $\delta >0$ and $C>0$ such that, for all $z\in \mathbb B_\delta ( ar z)$, $D_N\mathcal F (z)$ possesses full column rank $p$ such that  egin {equation}\label {eq:uniform_boundedness_eigenvalues} \lambda _	extup {min}(D_N\mathcal F (z)^	op D_N\mathcal F (z))\geq  rac {1}{C},\qquad 
orm {D_N\mathcal F (z)}\leq C. \end {equation} Then there exists $\varepsilon >0$ such that, for each starting point $z^0\in \mathbb B_\varepsilon ( ar z)$ and each null sequence $\{
u _k\}_{k\in \mathbb{N} }\subset (0,\varepsilon )$, \cref {alg:LocalLM} terminates after finitely many steps or produces a sequence $\{z^k\}_{k\in \mathbb{N} }$ which converges to $ ar z$ superlinearly. Furthermore, if $\mathcal F $ is even Newton-differentiable on $M$ of order $1$, and if $
u _k\in \mathpzc{O} (\Vert\mathcal F (z^k) \Vert)$ while $\mathcal F $ is calm at $ ar z$, then the convergence is quadratic.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Learned initializer + Gauss-Newton/LM posterior-mean refinement reaches near the Cramér–Rao floor
text: A noise-augmented MLP gives an initial estimate inside the local basin of the true k. Five to fifteen bounded LM iterations in log-k space, followed by importance-sampled posterior-mean estimation, will then reach val rel_l2 < 0.03. That is within about 1.6x of the CRB floor of 0.0186. It should also beat the best pure data-driven model by at least 30% relative, because the remaining error of the learned map is mostly approximation error, not noise. The forward operator F: k -> u(sensors, times) comes from an explicit FD scheme. Each time step is affine in k, so F is a polynomial in (k1..k4) and is C-infinity with a Lipschitz Jacobian on the box. The Fisher condition number is about 48 with 4 parameters, so J has full column rank and is moderately conditioned. Under these conditions Gauss-Newton/LM converges quadratically near the solution. The only obstacle is globalisation, which a learned initializer handles. The CRB shows k1 and k4 are weakly determined (2.2% and 1.8% relative std). Physically, the pulse starts at x=0.5, so little flux reaches the outer segments, and the Dirichlet ends drain heat there. For these components the box prior matters, so the posterior mean (MMSE) should beat the mode in rel_l2. The explicit FD scheme used by context.forward is stable (CFL satisfied) for all k in [0.5,2]^4, so F is smooth and bounded on the box The model is exact: training and test data were generated by the same forward map with i.i.d. Gaussian noise, sigma=1e-3 The MLP initializer error (expected roughly 0.04–0.08 rel_l2) lies inside the basin of quadratic convergence The Laplace approximation at the LM solution is adequate for importance sampling, since the posterior is near-Gaussian at sigma=1e-3 except where truncated by the box

assumptions: The explicit FD scheme used by context.forward is stable (CFL satisfied) for all k in [0.5,2]^4, so F is smooth and bounded on the box
The model is exact: training and test data were generated by the same forward map with i.i.d. Gaussian noise, sigma=1e-3
The MLP initializer error (expected roughly 0.04–0.08 rel_l2) lies inside the basin of quadratic convergence
The Laplace approximation at the LM solution is adequate for importance sampling, since the posterior is near-Gaussian at sigma=1e-3 except where truncated by the box
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of (a) the torch_mlp initializer alone, (b) the hybrid with estimator=mode, and (c) the hybrid with posterior_mean. The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following holds: (c) has val rel_l2 >= 0.03; (c) fails to beat (a) by >= 30% relative; or the per-sample LM final residual norm squared divided by (n_obs * sigma^2) exceeds 1.5 for more than 5% of samples, which would indicate convergence to non-global minima.
data.if_fails: If the initializer alone is already near 0.02, the learned map is effectively MMSE-optimal and refinement is unnecessary. If refinement leaves high-residual outliers, the misfit landscape has spurious minima. Those would most likely come from the k1/k4 interchange symmetry, or from compensation between an outer and an adjacent inner segment. In that case more starts or a sensitivity-weighted parameterisation is needed. If the mode beats the posterior mean, the Laplace/importance sampling is poorly calibrated near box boundaries.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Global identifiability on the box: forward-only multistart MLE/MMSE without any learning matches the hybrid
text: For this 4-parameter problem the data-misfit functional ||F(k) - y||^2 has a single basin on [0.5,2]^4 at sigma=1e-3. If so, a purely physics-based posterior-mean estimator started from the prior centre plus a few random starts reaches val rel_l2 < 0.03. It should also come within 10% relative of the hybrid of proposal 1. If multimodality exists, it will show up as a heavy tail of per-sample errors (>5% of samples with rel error > 0.1) concentrated where an outer segment has a low k. Each sensor sits in its own segment (grid indices 5, 15, 25, 35 with segment width 10). The early-time signal at each sensor is dominated by the local diffusivity of its own segment and that of the segment between it and the pulse. This suggests a triangular sensitivity structure that should exclude parameter-compensating ridges. The danger case is when k2 or k3 is small: the outer segments then receive little heat before the Dirichlet ends dominate, and k1 or k4 becomes nearly unobservable. This is what the CRB already indicates. This experiment directly tests the conjectured unimodality from a prior run (m-261109-54edbdef). It is also the control that tells us whether the learned initializer in proposal 1 is doing real work. The explicit FD forward map is stable and smooth on the whole box Starting from the prior centre in log space plus 3 extra random starts covers all basins, if there are several A Tikhonov weight of 0 combined with the posterior_mean estimator is enough to handle the box prior: importance sampling enforces the truncation, and no extra shrinkage is needed The per-sample cost of 4 starts x 30 iterations fits within the 120 s experiment limit when forwards are vectorised

assumptions: The explicit FD forward map is stable and smooth on the whole box
Starting from the prior centre in log space plus 3 extra random starts covers all basins, if there are several
A Tikhonov weight of 0 combined with the posterior_mean estimator is enough to handle the box prior: importance sampling enforces the truncation, and no extra shrinkage is needed
The per-sample cost of 4 starts x 30 iterations fits within the 120 s experiment limit when forwards are vectorised
data.falsifiable_test: Run on val and record per-sample rel error and normalised final residual. The hypothesis is falsified in either of two ways. (i) Val rel_l2 >= 0.03. (ii) More than 5% of samples have normalised residual chi^2/n > 1.5 or per-sample rel error > 0.1 while the hybrid of proposal 1 fits them; this would demonstrate non-global minima. Secondarily, if the outlier samples cluster at small k2 or k3, that confirms the shadowing mechanism.
data.if_fails: If it is much worse than the hybrid and has a heavy error tail, the landscape is multimodal or has flat valleys. That justifies learned initialisation and possibly an adaptive design such as weighting early-time samples. If it matches the hybrid, the problem is globally identifiable in practice, and the cheapest robust solution is forward-only inference. That would also confirm m-261109-54edbdef.

author: researcher-ml
title: Amortised MLP initializer + posterior-mean LM refinement (hybrid) attains near-CRB accuracy
text: A noise-augmented torch MLP trained on log-targets provides an initial estimate inside the basin of attraction of the per-sample least-squares optimum; a short bounded LM refinement in log-space through the forward model, followed by the importance-sampled posterior mean under the box prior, reduces val rel_l2 to within ~1.5x of the CRB floor (0.0186). We therefore predict a val rel_l2 below 0.035, which is under the 0.05 target. The diagnostics give a CRB rel_l2 floor of 0.0186 and a Fisher condition number of about 48. The model has only 4 parameters, so the problem is locally well posed. Prior memory (m-261109-836f0093) conjectured that amortised MLPs alone stall above the CRB. Learned maps carry an approximation error that grows with ill-conditioning (k1 and k4 are weakly determined because sensors 5 and 35 sit near the Dirichlet ends). Gauss-Newton refinement removes that approximation error. Under squared loss, the posterior mean is the Bayes-optimal estimator, which matters for k1 and k4, whose posteriors are truncated at the box edges. The posterior-mean argument follows from the Bayes-rule statement in ts:thm:24457901, which holds for the point-estimate part. The MLP init error is small enough (rel err well under 0.2) that 15 LM iterations converge to the global minimiser. The local Laplace approximation is adequate for importance sampling at sigma=0.001. The forward-model budget allows roughly 750 samples x ~20 iterations x Jacobian calls within 120 s across 6 workers. rel_l2 is computed as an aggregate norm ratio, so errors on k1 and k4 dominate.

assumptions: The MLP init error is small enough (rel err well under 0.2) that 15 LM iterations converge to the global minimiser.
The local Laplace approximation is adequate for importance sampling at sigma=0.001.
The forward-model budget allows roughly 750 samples x ~20 iterations x Jacobian calls within 120 s across 6 workers.
rel_l2 is computed as an aggregate norm ratio, so errors on k1 and k4 dominate.
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid against its own MLP initializer, which the harness logs. The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid val rel_l2 is at or above 0.035, or if it improves on the initializer by less than 25%.
data.if_fails: If the hybrid gains little over the MLP, the amortised map is already close to MMSE and the residual error is noise-limited. If the hybrid is worse than the MLP, LM is converging to spurious minima or drifting to the box bounds on k1 and k4. Either outcome tells us whether to increase tikhonov or switch the estimator to mode.

author: researcher-ml
title: Amortised MMSE: a noise-augmented MLP on PCA-compressed traces reaches the 0.05 target without any forward-model calls at inference
text: A squared-loss MLP trained on simulated data, with on-the-fly noise augmentation at the true sigma, approximates E[k | y]. With PCA-48 whitened features it achieves val rel_l2 below 0.05 without any per-sample physics. We expect it to remain at least 1.3x worse than the hybrid, with the gap concentrated in k1 and k4. Amortisation is our core ML question: does a learned inverse map alone succeed on a 4-parameter, well-conditioned problem? With noise augmentation, the population minimiser of squared loss is the posterior mean, because the training pairs are drawn from the joint prior-likelihood. The remaining risk is approximation and estimation error from 3000 samples. PCA keeps the dominant signal subspace, discards noise-only directions, and improves conditioning for the MLP. Prior memory entries m-261109-742270b6 and m-261109-e8113fbb indicate earlier runs tested variants of this, and a critique flagged the hybrid gap. This proposal isolates that gap so we can quantify the value of the physics refinement. 3000 training samples suffice for a smooth 4-output map. The posterior is near-Gaussian, so E[k|y] is smooth in y. The first 48 PCA components capture essentially all of the Fisher information (only 4 informative directions plus nonlinearity). Noise augmentation at sigma=0.001 matches the test noise distribution.

assumptions: 3000 training samples suffice for a smooth 4-output map. The posterior is near-Gaussian, so E[k|y] is smooth in y.
The first 48 PCA components capture essentially all of the Fisher information (only 4 informative directions plus nonlinearity).
Noise augmentation at sigma=0.001 matches the test noise distribution.
data.falsifiable_test: The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 is at or above 0.05. Separately, the predicted 1.3x gap is falsified if the hybrid from proposal 1 is not at least 1.3x better. Per-parameter errors should be checked to confirm whether k1 and k4 dominate.
data.if_fails: If val rel_l2 is at or above 0.05, the amortised map is limited by data or approximation error, not by noise. Physics refinement (proposal 1) or simulating extra training data via context.forward would then be necessary. If it reaches the target close to the hybrid, the physics refinement adds little at this noise level.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Metric-matched hybrid: noise-augmented MLP initializer plus LM refinement with posterior-mean readout reaches near the CRB floor
text: Sensor noise (sigma=0.001) is small relative to the sensor-signal sensitivity, so the per-sample posterior is close to Gaussian over most of the prior box. In that regime a learned initializer followed by a few bounded log-space Levenberg-Marquardt iterations through the exact forward model lands in the global basin. An MMSE (posterior_mean) readout under the box prior then achieves val rel_l2 within about 1.5x of the CRB estimate (0.0186), i.e. below 0.03. The remaining excess error should sit mainly in k1 and k4, the least determined parameters. The diagnostics put the information floor at rel_l2 about 0.019, well below the 0.05 target, so the limiting factor is the estimator, not the data. Simulated and real observations come from the same explicit finite-difference solver with known initial and boundary conditions, so there is no simulation-fidelity gap and the forward model is exact up to noise. The learned initializer removes the multistart cost and the risk of local minima. The posterior-mean readout matches the squared-error metric and shrinks k1 and k4 toward the interior where the box prior truncates the likelihood. The context.forward simulator is identical to the generator of the train, val and test features, so there is no model discrepancy. The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=0.001; there is no hidden bias or correlated noise. The MLP initializer lands inside the basin of the global minimum for nearly all samples (init error well under about 0.2 relative). The Laplace approximation is adequate for importance sampling, apart from posterior mass truncated at the box edges for k1 and k4. author: researcher-experimental
title: Noise-model fidelity control: an amortised MLP is only as good as its training noise match; matched-noise augmentation is necessary and sufficient for the 0.05
text: A squared-loss network trained on simulated traces corrupted with noise of the correct statistics (i.i.d. Gaussian, sigma=0.001, matched to the test features) approximates the posterior mean and reaches val rel_l2 < 0.05 without the forward model at inference. The competing explanation is that the remaining error is approximation error from finite training data (3000 samples in 4D) rather than a noise mismatch. That explanation predicts no gain from augmentation; mine predicts that an augmented run clearly beats an otherwise identical non-augmented run. From a measurement-design view, the inverse map is only as well learned as the training distribution matches the measurement distribution. If train features already carry one noise draw each, augmentation supplies fresh noise realisations per sample and regularises toward the Bayes estimator. This is the cheap amortised control arm that tells us how much the physics refinement in proposal 1 actually adds. A log target transform respects positivity and the multiplicative character of conductivity errors. noise_scale is interpreted in units of the stated noise_std (1.0 means sigma=0.001); if it is in feature units after scaling, the effective noise is mis-set and the test becomes about calibration. Train features are generated by the same simulator and noise process as val and test. 3000 samples cover the 4D prior box well enough for an MLP to interpolate smoothly. The paired comparison uses the same seed and architecture, so the only difference is noise_aug.

Train features are generated by the same simulator and noise process as val and test.
3000 samples cover the 4D prior box well enough for an MLP to interpolate smoothly.

data.falsifiable_test:
1. Run this spec and an identical spec with noise_aug=0 (paired seed).
2. Report val rel_l2 and the per-parameter error for both runs.
3. The hypothesis is falsified if either holds:
   - the augmented run has val rel_l2 >= 0.05;
   - augmentation improves rel_l2 by less than 10% relative, which would favour the approximation-error explanation.
4. As a secondary check, the per-parameter error ranking should mirror the CRB ranking (k1 and k4 worst). A different ranking points to network bias rather than information limits.
data.if_fails: If both arms are above 0.05 with a negligible augmentation gain, the bottleneck is sample size or capacity; the forward model should then be used to simulate more training data or to refine via LM (proposal 1). If the error ranking does not follow the CRB, inspect the noise_scale semantics and the feature scaling for a measurement-model mismatch.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Truncated-prior MMSE can undercut the CRB 'floor': amortised init plus a forward-model posterior-mean refinement
text: The harness CRB estimate (rel_l2 about 0.0186) bounds only unbiased estimators. k1 and k4 are poorly determined (CR rel std 0.022 and 0.018) relative to the prior box [0.5, 2]. So a box-prior posterior mean, computed by importance sampling on the Laplace approximation around an LM-refined amortised initialiser, should reach val rel_l2 below 0.020 and plausibly at or below 0.0186. It should also clearly beat the pure-amortised MLP (0.026). Challenge the framing that the CRB is a floor. The metric is squared-error-like, and the prior is a known, bounded uniform box. A biased Bayes estimator trades variance for bias exactly where the Fisher information is weakest, especially for samples whose k1 or k4 lies near a bound. Prior memory m-261109-28420efa conjectured this init-plus-MMSE combination but has no recorded outcome. This experiment tests it, and also tests the specific claim that it breaks the unbiased bound. The Laplace approximation at the LM optimum is accurate enough for importance sampling. Noise sigma=1e-3 is small, so the posterior is near-Gaussian except where truncated by the box. The MLP initialiser lands inside the basin of the global LS minimum, so 15 LM iterations converge. The harness forward and Jacobian calls on the 750 val (and later test) samples fit in the 120 s per-experiment limit. Optimising in log-k space improves LM conditioning because the conductivities enter multiplicatively in the flux.

data.if_fails: Suppose refinement reaches about 0.0186 but not below it. Then the box truncation is too rarely active to matter, and MLE-level accuracy is the practical ceiling. Then either LM convergence is failing (initialiser outside the basin, or a too-small iteration budget) or the forward model mismatches the data-generating simulator. That would deserve its own check: a residual-norm-versus-noise chi-square test.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: The amortised-network gap is a data-scarcity artefact, not a noise floor: simulation-augmented training through the forward model
text: The MLP plateau at about 0.026 is caused by having only 3000 training pairs for a 4-D inverse map, not by the measurement noise. Adding about 12000 freshly simulated prior draws, each with a fresh N(0, 1e-3) noise realisation, should cut val rel_l2 to below 0.023 without any per-sample optimisation at inference time. This is a learned MMSE estimator, because squared loss on noisy simulations targets the posterior mean. This challenges the framing that the provided train split is the dataset. The forward model is a free, prior-matched simulator, so amortised inference can use simulation-based inference with unlimited draws. The test also separates two explanations for the MLP-to-CRB gap: approximation and estimation error, which shrinks with n, versus the irreducible Bayes error, which does not. It tests memory hypothesis m-261109-d9e17446 under a stronger data regime. context.forward is the same simulator that generated the train, val and test features, with the same feature layout. The code guards on shape and falls back to the original data otherwise. The forward budget allows about 12000 evaluations. If the call fails, the method silently reverts to plain training, which is itself informative. Simulated data drawn from the stated uniform prior is admissible under the constraint 'models may only be trained on simulated data'. 48 PCA components keep nearly all of the parameter-relevant signal, given that the data are smooth heat-kernel traces.

If instead PCA discards Fisher-informative low-variance directions, the loss will show up specifically in k1 and k4. We would then see a per-parameter rel err ratio (PCA/raw) above 1.15 for k1/k4 and close to 1 for k2/k3. The pilot gives 0.0478 at n_train=300, so the amortised map already clears the target with little data. The open ML question is whether input representation limits the result. The observation vector has about 800 dimensions (4 sensors x ~200 times) but only 4 parameters, so the informative manifold is low-dimensional. Pairing this arm with P-006 (raw) isolates the representation effect at almost no extra design cost. P-006 runs with raw features, log-y and comparable augmentation. The contrast is confounded only by aug2 versus aug3, which I take to be a second-order effect once augmentation matches the true sigma. noise_scale=1.0 means augmentation noise at 1x the true sigma=0.001.
